English
I created UdaraKita, a web app that monitors and predicts air quality (US AQI) for 12 Indonesian cities. An XGBoost model predicts tomorrow’s AQI from pollutant data (PM2.5, PM10, ozone, NO₂, SO₂, CO), recent AQI history, and seasonal patterns. Results appear with a health category, a prediction range, BMKG and Open-Meteo weather, an interactive map, and three languages (Indonesian, English, Japanese). I built it with FastAPI and React and deployed it on Vercel.

Results: 11 of 12 cities beat the “tomorrow = today” baseline by at least 15%, with an average error reduction of about 29% (best: Makassar, 39%). Jakarta’s error is 8.9 AQI points versus 11.9 for the baseline. The one city that did not pass (Semarang, 11%) does not show a prediction.

Most mobile chat tutorials rely on Firebase or third-party cloud SDKs.

I decided to build a full-stack WhatsApp alternative completely from scratch — sub-50ms latency, zero Firebase, and verified cross-platform parity on Apple iOS and Google Android. ⚡

During my Mobile Application Development (HHDP 1) module, I built Tappsy: pairing the proven UX patterns of WhatsApp (Chats/Updates/Calls tabs, speech bubbles with directional tails, double blue ticks ✓✓, status story rings) with an electric brand identity (#0084FF).

💡 Key Engineering Highlights:
• Instant Sub-50ms Messaging: Bidirectional WebSockets (wss://) hosted on a native Java EE / Jakarta EE server (@ServerEndpoint), eliminating polling overhead and conserving mobile battery life.
• Resilient Socket Engine: Custom client-side heartbeat loop (Ping/Pong) with exponential backoff to handle mobile network handovers cleanly.
• Dual-Theme Parity: Complete Light (#FFFFFF) and Dark Mode (#0F172A Slate) styling dynamically syncing with system appearance via custom ThemeProvider & NativeWind.
• End-to-End Onboarding: Animated flow with country-code dialing (+94 Sri Lanka defaults), SHA-256 PIN security, and multipart avatar uploads.
• Dual-Platform Verification: Captured live on both Apple iOS Simulator (iPhone 18 Pro) and Google Android Emulator (Pixel 9a).

posts.text:
One of the fastest ways to trigger a React hydration mismatch in a Next.js App Router application is a single line of date formatting code.

Everything looks completely normal on your local machine. Then you deploy to production, and the browser console throws a hydration error while dates briefly flicker on mobile screens.

Here is why it happens:
Your Next.js Server Component renders the HTML on a Vercel server running in UTC time. When the user opens the page in Jakarta, Sydney, or London, their browser runs client-side hydration using their local timezone and locale settings.

If your component calls new Date().toLocaleDateString() directly during render, the server output and the browser output do not match. React rejects the mismatch and forces an expensive client re-render.

Here are three clean ways we eliminate timezone hydration bugs in production:

1. Lock the Timezone Explicitly on Both Sides:
Never rely on implicit default locales inside Intl.DateTimeFormat or toLocaleDateString. Pass both the locale and an explicit timeZone parameter (for example, 'en-US' and 'UTC' or a stored user timezone preference from the database) so the server and browser produce the exact same string.

2. Defer Local User Timezone Formatting Until Mount:
If you genuinely need the visitor's local browser clock (like "2 hours ago" or local event times), render a deterministic fallback or ISO date on the server, then update to the local string inside a small isolated client wrapper after mount. Never wrap an entire page in a mounted check just to format a timestamp.

3. Pass Serialized ISO Strings Across Server-Client Boundaries:
Pass plain ISO strings from Server Components into Client Components instead of raw Date instances or pre-formatted strings that drop timezone offsets.

Hydration bugs rarely come from complicated business logic. Nine times out of ten, they come from small assumptions about browser globals like window, Date, or invalid nested HTML tags.

A $698 million bilateral grant. A strict five-year execution clock. Zero extensions. 

When major international development compacts and blended-finance facilities enter into force in Indonesia, the celebration at the signing ceremony quickly collides with a hard operational reality. The countdown clock is ticking, and every unspent dollar at the five-year mark goes back to the donor treasury. 

Yet across Southeast Asia, flagship infrastructure and financial-inclusion programs routinely stall in their first 24 months. With single-digit disbursement rates early on, Project Management Units get trapped between two worlds. They struggle to synchronize rigid international donor procurement and monitoring standards with Indonesia's complex inter-ministerial, sub-national (Pemda), and state-budget (APBN) machinery. 

Unlocking hundreds of millions of dollars in regional transport logistics, capital market blended finance, and MSME credit does not require another macroeconomic white paper. It requires an Executive Control Tower capable of forcing alignment across ministries, local governments, commercial lenders, and civil society before the clock runs out.

🚀 Excited to share that I’ll be presenting our research at the AAPG International Conference & Exhibition (ICE) 2026, taking place on 7–9 December 2026 in Jakarta, Indonesia!

Our research is titled:
“CFD-FEM-Based Optimization of Sand Control in Mature Fields Incorporating Geological Factors and Economic Analysis: A Case Study of Duri and Minas Reservoirs.”

Sand production remains a challenge in mature oil fields, affecting production performance, equipment reliability, and operating costs. Our study integrates computational fluid dynamics (CFD), finite element modelling (FEM), geological factors, and economic analysis to evaluate sand control strategies for the Duri and Minas reservoirs.

By connecting geological conditions with mechanical performance and economic considerations, this research aims to support more informed sand control decisions.

📅 8 December 2026
🕙 10:00–10:30 AM WIB (Jakarta time)
📍 Exhibition Hall, Nusantara International Convention Exhibition (NICE)

I’m grateful to my research team and everyone who has contributed their time, insights, and support throughout this work.

🤝 Attending ICE 2026? Stop by our poster! I’d love to exchange ideas with fellow engineers, geoscientists, researchers, and industry professionals on sand control, simulation, and mature field optimization.

The cost of building scalable software is not the developer hours.

A founder gets a quote built on salaries or sprint estimates. Then the real bills arrive, and none of them were in it.

Four that rarely make the budget:

1. Infrastructure. Egress and cross-zone transfer can outweigh compute in data-heavy systems. Flexera's 2024 report found companies waste up to 32% of their cloud spend.

2. Operations. A team of five that spends 30% of its time on monitoring, patching and incidents is really a team of 3.5 building features.

3. Early mistakes. One marketplace chose its inventory data model in two days. Past 500,000 SKUs it took six weeks and three production incidents to fix.

4. Knowledge. When a lead backend engineer left a Jakarta startup, a database migration stopped for three weeks.

Compliance is the fifth. Retrofitting audit logs and access controls costs far more than building them in.

"How much will the developers cost?" is the wrong first question. Ask what it will cost to run, to change, and to hand over.

I wrote up a cost model with the numbers to use as a floor. Link in the first comment.
